newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Asia-Pacific economic growth seen at 4 pct in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Asia-Pacific economic growth seen at 4 pct in 1996.

text.p: The economies of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum are in robust health, with total output estimated to grow by about four percent this year, the group said in a report on Friday.
With a combined annual income of $13 trillion, the 18 member economies of APEC accounted for 55 percent of total world income and 40 percent of global trade in 1995, the report said.

"The fastest growing economies are experiencing a moderation of growth, while the slowest growing economies have seen significant recoveries," the APEC Economic Committee said in a report released at the group's annual conference.
Projected growth rates ranged from a low of 1.5 percent in Canada to China's 9.5 percent.
Some of the fastest growing economies -- Chile, China, Malaysia and South Korea -- are projected to avoid overheating as growth slows to more sustainable levels.
Other economies that have experienced downturns are now picking up, most notably in Japan, the Philippines and Mexico, which is recovering from a liquidity crisis, the report said.
The moderating growth has kept inflation in check.

"Inflation is falling in a number of countries, most dramatically in China and Mexico. Inflation has edged upward slightly in only a few economies and does not appear to be increasing significantly in any APEC country," the report said.
For the region as a whole, the rate of inflation was at 6.3 percent in 1995. But the 1995 inflation rate of 0.1 percent in Japan contrasted sharply with Mexico's 52 percent rate.
The strong growth throughout APEC, sometimes accompanied by spurts of strong short-term capital inflows, has shifted macroeconomic risks from recession to inflation, the report said.
"More restrictive monetary policies in some economies can be expected in the near future," it said.
Large current account deficits remain a concern in Indonesia, Thailand and Malaysia, although the external imbalances have not spurred inflationary pressures, the report said.
While export growth has slowed in much of Asia, it remains strong in the Philippines and Mexico -- which both posted around 20 percent growth rates in 1996.
Some of the factors in slower export growth -- excess supplies of electronic goods and appreciating real exchange rates -- are likely to be temporary, the report said.
The report looked at efforts to establish environmental and agricultural policies that would promote sustainable growth.
"The value of many resources -- such as fish populations, clean air and forests -- is not appropriately priced in the market; the result is often overharvesting, degradation and denudation," it said.
The report noted a strong link between education and growth. Each additional year of schooling is thought to raise future earnings by five to 15 percent, according to studies in the United States.
In the "miracle" economies of East Asia, primary education was the most important factor behind high growth rates over the past 30 years or so, a World Bank study found.
Strong growth has had a profound impact on labour, with more and more women joining the workforce and armies of migrant workers being lured across borders to service booming economies.
Lower transportation costs have greatly boosted migrant labourers. At least 125 million people now live outside their economy of origin, the report said.
Asian countries that once exported labour -- South Korea, Malaysia and Taiwan, for instance -- are now net importers.
Migrants are often more productive and reduce labour losts in the host economy. Labour exporting countries reap considerable gains through remittances their workers send home, it said.
